lessons.title: Set up Cursor Tab and get completions worth keeping
lessons.summary: Install Cursor, pick the right plan, and learn the habits that turn Tab's multi-edit predictions from noise into a real speed boost.
lessons.goal: Get Cursor installed and configured, and learn to read, accept, and reject Tab's inline and next-edit suggestions deliberately instead of by reflex.
lessons.whyItMatters: Tab is the feature you'll use dozens of times an hour in Cursor, so the habits you build in week one — accepting blindly or reading critically — compound across your whole career with the tool. Getting the plan right also determines whether you're on Hobby's tighter usage or a paid plan with a full model-usage budget.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Cursor account, and either the free Hobby tier or a paid plan (Pro is $20/mo with roughly $20 of included model usage).
steps: Download Cursor from cursor.com and sign in — it's a fork of VS Code, so it can import your existing VS Code extensions, keybindings, and settings on first launch.
Check your plan under Cursor Settings > Billing — Hobby is free with limited usage, Pro ($20/mo) includes a pool of model usage with caching, and higher tiers (Pro+, Ultra) raise that pool further.
Open a real file in a real project — not a scratch file — since Tab's suggestions improve with genuine surrounding context and codebase indexing.
Start a new function with a descriptive name and, if the logic isn't obvious from the name alone, a one-line comment above it.
Watch for the greyed-out ghost-text suggestion that appears as you type; press Tab to accept it, or Esc to dismiss it.

Notice when Tab predicts more than one change at once — it can suggest edits at several points in the file for a single action, and pressing Tab again jumps you to the next predicted edit site instead of just inserting text at the cursor.
Read every accepted suggestion line by line before moving on — a Tab completion is a draft, not a verified answer.
lessons.explanation: Tab predicts what comes next based on everything visible around the cursor — plus, on an indexed codebase, patterns from files you haven't even opened — so the quality of what you type first sets the ceiling for what it can suggest. A descriptive function name tells it the goal; a short comment states the contract (inputs, outputs, edge cases) in plain language; and the open brace signals it's time to generate a body, not more comments. The zero-rate edge case called out explicitly is the single most common bug in a naive completion of this function, so naming it up front is what makes the difference between a plausible-looking answer and a correct one.
lessons.example:
Input: the signature and comment above, left with the cursor after the opening brace.

Typical output: a suggested body that destructures the three parameters, converts the annual rate to a monthly decimal rate, applies the standard amortization formula, checks for the annualRatePercent === 0 case first, and returns the result rounded to two decimal places — matching every constraint stated in the comment, because the comment stated them.
lessons.exercise: In your own Cursor account, open a real file in a project you're working on. Write a new function with a descriptive name and a 2-3 line comment describing its inputs, outputs, and one edge case. Let Tab suggest the body, and only accept the version that actually handles your stated edge case — editing the specific wrong part if it's close but not quite right.
lessons.expectedResult: A working function body that matches your comment's contract, which you can explain line by line because you read it before accepting.
commonMistakes: Accepting the first suggestion on reflex without reading it, then discovering the edge-case bug in code review instead of at write time.
Writing vague function names like `process` or `handle`, which gives Tab nothing to anchor a specific suggestion on.
Working in an empty scratch file, which strips away the surrounding context and codebase index Tab would otherwise use.
Assuming the Hobby plan's usage limits mean lower-quality suggestions — the underlying models are the same; only how much you can use before hitting a cap differs.
lessons.proTip: If a suggestion is almost right but wrong in one spot, don't retype the whole line — edit just the wrong part and keep typing. Tab re-suggests the rest based on your correction, which is usually faster than rejecting and waiting for a fresh suggestion.

lessons.title: Steer Cursor Tab with comments, open files, and codebase context
lessons.summary: Learn what Tab actually reads before suggesting code — open tabs, nearby comments, existing patterns, and your whole indexed codebase — so you can deliberately shape suggestions instead of hoping for the best.
lessons.goal: Control what Tab suggests by managing its context: which files are open, how you comment intent, how consistently your existing code establishes a pattern, and when to move a preference into a standing Rule instead of repeating it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Once you know Tab's suggestions are built from your current file, your open editor tabs, recently edited files, and Cursor's index of your whole codebase, bad or off-pattern completions stop feeling random. You can fix most of them by changing what's in front of it — and for anything you'd otherwise have to restate in every session, a short Rule fixes it once instead of every time.
steps: Before starting a task, open the 2-3 files most relevant to it in editor tabs — Tab weighs open and recently edited files more heavily than the rest of the indexed codebase.
For any function whose purpose isn't obvious from its name, add a one- or two-line comment above it stating intent before you start typing the body.
When behavior is ambiguous, add a concrete input/output example in the comment instead of a longer prose description.

Write your first instance of a repeated pattern (e.g. the first API route handler, the first test) carefully and completely — Tab mimics established patterns for every similar block after it, whether or not the file is open.
If a suggestion drifts off in the wrong direction, delete it, add an explicit type signature or JSDoc annotation, and retrigger by typing a character.

For a whole class of repetitive code (e.g. five similar test cases), accept the first one fully, then let Tab draft the rest — but check every occurrence individually, since 'similar' isn't 'identical.'
Close irrelevant tabs from unrelated features before a focused task — even with codebase indexing, open files pull suggestions toward their pattern first.

If you find yourself typing the same comment or convention reminder in file after file, that's a signal to move it into a `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` file instead — a standing Rule applies automatically without you retyping it (covered fully in a later lesson).
lessons.prompt:
/**
 * formatCurrency
 * @param {number} amountCents - amount in integer cents, e.g. 1050 for $10.50
 * @param {string} currencyCode - ISO 4217 code, e.g. "USD", "EUR"
 * @returns {string} localized display string, e.g. "$10.50"
 * @example formatCurrency(1050, "USD") // "$10.50"
 * @example formatCurrency(99, "EUR") // "€0.99"
 */
lessons.promptLabel: Example JSDoc block with worked examples
lessons.explanation: The @example lines do more work than a paragraph of description because they pin down the exact input/output shape — including the cents-to-decimal conversion and the currency symbol placement — leaving no room for Tab to guess wrong on formatting. JSDoc's typed @param tags also constrain the argument types directly, which matters more than plain-English context once a function takes more than one argument of the same primitive type.
lessons.example:
Input: the JSDoc block above with the cursor on the next line.

Typical output: a function body that reads amountCents, divides by 100, and formats it via Intl.NumberFormat with the given currencyCode — reproducing both worked examples exactly, because the examples removed every formatting decision Tab would otherwise have had to guess.
lessons.exercise: Pick a function in your own project whose last Tab suggestion was wrong or off-pattern. Open the 1-2 files it should have taken its pattern from, add a comment with one concrete input/output example, and retrigger the suggestion. Compare it to the original attempt.
lessons.expectedResult: A suggestion that matches your stated example exactly, or is close enough that fixing the remaining gap takes seconds rather than a rewrite.
commonMistakes: Writing a long prose comment instead of a concrete example — Tab follows a worked example more reliably than an abstract description.
Leaving unrelated files open from a different feature, which can pull suggestions toward that feature's patterns instead of the current one.
Writing the first instance of a repeated pattern sloppily, then being surprised every later suggestion copies the sloppiness.
Retyping the same convention reminder in comment after comment instead of writing it once as a Rule that applies everywhere automatically.
lessons.proTip: When a whole file follows a strict convention (e.g. every exported function has a matching test), open the test file and the implementation file side by side — Tab will often draft the test to match the implementation's actual behavior instead of a generic template.

lessons.title: Get unblocked on unfamiliar code fast: Cursor Chat or Claude Code, whichever fits
lessons.summary: Learn the judgment call between a quick in-editor question in Cursor Chat and a dedicated investigation in Claude Code, plus the team habit of writing down what you find so nobody re-derives it.
lessons.goal: Use Cursor Chat and Claude Code to explain, trace, and question unfamiliar code — and choose the right one for the situation instead of defaulting to whichever tool happens to be open.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every developer inherits code they didn't write: a legacy module, a teammate's PR, a dependency's internals. Both Cursor Chat and Claude Code can turn that from a slow read-and-guess process into a conversation, but they're built for different moments — a quick clarifying question mid-task versus a genuine standalone investigation — and picking the wrong one either interrupts your flow or under-powers a hard question. A team that writes down what it finds also stops paying the same investigation cost twice.
steps: If you're already mid-task in Cursor and just need one clarifying answer, open Cursor Chat and @-mention the file or selection rather than switching tools — it's faster and keeps your place.

If the question is genuinely a standalone investigation (tracing a bug across several files, understanding a subsystem before a big change), start a dedicated Claude Code session instead — its read-only exploration and Plan Mode are built for open-ended search without editing anything by accident.
In Cursor Chat, select the function you don't understand and @-mention it directly, or reference the whole file with @filename, then ask a specific question, not "what does this do."
In Claude Code, ask the same kind of specific question in plain language, or explicitly say "just explore and report back, don't edit anything" to keep it read-only.
Ask follow-up questions in the same thread or session rather than starting over, in either tool.
For a repo you don't have open locally, use Claude Code on the web (claude.ai/code) against the GitHub repo directly, or a Cursor remote session.
Treat every explanation as a hypothesis to verify against the actual code, not a verified fact.
Once you have the answer, paste a two- or three-line summary into the PR description, issue, or team channel — the next person who hits the same question shouldn't have to run the same investigation.
lessons.prompt: Explain what this function does, focusing specifically on: what happens if `items` is empty, whether this function mutates its input array, and any place elsewhere in this file that calls it without checking the return value for null.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable question — paste into Cursor Chat with the function selected, or a Claude Code session
lessons.explanation: The three named follow-ups — empty input, mutation, unchecked callers — convert a vague 'what does this do' into specific questions with verifiable answers, in either tool. In Cursor Chat, selecting the function or @-mentioning it anchors the answer to the exact code you're worried about instead of the whole file; in Claude Code, stating the question plainly (or explicitly asking it to explore without editing) gets the same anchoring without a special syntax. Asking for callers elsewhere in the file also pushes either tool to actually search, not just describe the selected block in isolation.
lessons.example:
Input: a 40-line data-transformation function, selected in Cursor or referenced in a Claude Code session, with the prompt above.

Typical output: a paragraph explaining the transformation logic, a specific note that an empty `items` array returns an empty result without throwing, a note on whether the array is mutated in place or copied, and a list of two call sites in the file that don't check the return value — each one worth checking by hand.
lessons.exercise: Pick a function in your own project you're not fully sure about. If you're already mid-task in Cursor, ask in Cursor Chat with the function selected. If it's a standalone investigation — tracing a bug, understanding a subsystem before a big change — open a fresh Claude Code session instead and ask the same question, telling it explicitly not to edit anything. Verify the answer yourself, then write the two-line summary you'd actually paste into a PR or team channel.
lessons.expectedResult: A clear, specific explanation you can verify against the code in under a minute, plus a short written note a teammate could read instead of re-running the same investigation.
commonMistakes: Asking 'what does this code do' with nothing selected or referenced, which produces a vague answer instead of an explanation of the part you actually care about.
Treating the explanation as ground truth instead of a claim to verify — either tool can misread control flow just like a human skimming quickly.

Defaulting to whichever tool is already open out of habit — launching a full Claude Code session for a one-line question Cursor Chat would answer in seconds, or trying to force a genuine multi-file investigation into a quick in-editor chat.
Finding the answer and never writing it down anywhere a teammate could find it later, so the next person re-runs the exact same investigation.
lessons.proTip: When exploring a repo you've just joined, ask the same module two ways: once for 'what does this do' and once for 'why would someone have written it this way instead of the obvious alternative' — the second question surfaces constraints and history a comment never would, in either tool.

lessons.title: Delegate a scoped multi-file change and review it like a PR
lessons.summary: Scope a small feature that spans several files, choose Cursor Agent, Claude Code, or a Codex cloud task depending on how hands-on you need to be, and review every diff before accepting.
lessons.goal: Scope a small multi-file change, pick the agent surface that matches how hands-on you need to be, and review the resulting diffs file by file before accepting anything.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most real features touch more than one file. Cursor Agent and an interactive Claude Code session run in front of you so you can watch and redirect mid-task; Codex cloud tasks and a Claude Code background or worktree session run unattended and hand back a finished PR. Picking the wrong mode for the moment either wastes your attention babysitting something that didn't need it, or leaves you unable to redirect something that's already gone off track. Either way, it only saves time if you review the output like a colleague's PR, not rubber-stamp it.
steps: Decide up front how hands-on you need to be: if you want to watch it work and redirect mid-task, use Cursor Agent or an interactive Claude Code session; if the task is well-specified enough to walk away from, use a Codex cloud task or a Claude Code background/worktree session.
Describe the change in terms of behavior and scope, not implementation: what should work afterward, and which files or directories are in bounds.

Let the agent propose a plan first — Claude Code's Plan Mode, Cursor Agent's up-front plan, or a Codex task's description of what it intends to do — and read it before it starts writing; stop it if the scope is already wrong.
Review each file's diff individually as it's produced — accept, reject, or ask for a change per file rather than approving the whole batch at once.
Run your test suite (or ask the agent to run it) after the edits land, and treat a passing suite as a starting point for manual review, not proof of correctness.
If a diff touches a file you didn't expect, ask why before accepting it — unexpected scope creep is the most common failure mode across all three tools.
If you're running an unattended task, check back deliberately rather than assuming silence means success — read the final diff with the same attention you'd give a live session.
Commit in a single reviewed unit once you're satisfied, so the change is easy to revert as a whole if something surfaces later.
lessons.prompt:
Add a `/api/orders/:id/cancel` endpoint.

Scope: only touch src/routes/orders.ts, src/services/orderService.ts, and their existing test files. Do not modify the database schema or add new dependencies.

Behavior: only orders with status "pending" or "processing" can be cancelled; anything else returns a 409 with a clear error message. On success, set status to "cancelled" and return the updated order. Add test cases for the valid-cancel path, the invalid-status path, and the not-found path.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable task description — works as a Cursor Agent prompt, a Claude Code instruction, or a Codex task
lessons.explanation: Naming the exact files in bounds stops any of the three agents from touching migrations or unrelated services it technically could reach. Stating the behavior as business rules rather than code gives it room to write idiomatic code matching the existing service's style instead of a pattern you dictated by hand. Requesting the three specific test cases turns 'add an endpoint' into something you can verify mechanically — and none of that discipline depends on which of the three tools you hand it to.
lessons.example:
Input: the task above, run as a Cursor Agent session against a small Express-style API (the same task works unchanged as a Claude Code instruction or a Codex cloud task).

Typical output: a diff to orderService.ts adding a cancelOrder method with the status check, a diff to orders.ts wiring the new route, and a diff to the test file with three new test cases — each reviewable independently, with the agent explaining its status-check logic inline before you accept.
lessons.exercise: Pick a small feature in a side project or sandbox repo that genuinely touches 2-3 files. Decide first whether you want to watch it happen or hand it off entirely — choose Cursor Agent or interactive Claude Code for the former, a Codex cloud task or Claude Code background session for the latter — scope it explicitly by filename, and review every file's diff separately before accepting.
lessons.expectedResult: A multi-file change where you can explain what each individual diff does and why, produced by whichever tool matched how hands-on you needed to be, with no file touched outside the scope you named.
commonMistakes: Approving a whole multi-file diff at once without reading each file, which is exactly how scope creep and unrelated changes slip into a commit unnoticed.
Describing the task purely in implementation terms, which gives the agent no room to make good local decisions and often produces code that doesn't match the file's existing style.
Not naming files or directories that are off-limits, so the agent 'helpfully' touches a shared utility or config file you didn't want changed.
Choosing an unattended surface — a Codex cloud task or a background session — for a task that turns out to be genuinely ambiguous, and only discovering the wrong turn once it's already finished.
lessons.proTip: For anything touching more than 4-5 files, split it into two smaller requests instead of one large one, regardless of which tool you're using — smaller scopes are easier to review honestly, and a bad plan is cheaper to catch early.

lessons.title: Turn a GitHub issue into a reviewed PR with Codex cloud tasks or Claude Code
lessons.summary: Write a well-scoped GitHub issue, delegate it to a Codex cloud task or a Claude Code session tied to the repo, and review the pull request it opens with the same rigor as a human contributor's work.
lessons.goal: Turn a properly scoped GitHub issue into a pull request by delegating it to a Codex cloud task or Claude Code, then review the PR with the same rigor you'd apply to a human contributor's work.
lessons.whyItMatters: Both Codex cloud tasks and Claude Code sessions can work asynchronously in an isolated sandbox, so you can delegate a well-defined task and come back to a draft PR instead of babysitting a session. The quality of the issue you write is the single biggest predictor of the quality of the PR you get back, whichever of the two you hand it to — this is the highest-leverage skill in this whole path for anyone managing more than their own tasks.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A GitHub repository connected to Codex Cloud (chatgpt.com/codex) or to Claude Code (via claude.ai/code or the GitHub Actions integration), and a ChatGPT or Claude plan that includes agentic usage.
steps: Write the issue like a spec, not a one-line request: describe the problem, the expected behavior, and explicit acceptance criteria.
State scope boundaries directly in the issue — which files or modules are in play, and anything that must not change (schema, public API, dependencies).

Hand it off: connect the repo at chatgpt.com/codex and describe the task for a Codex cloud task, which runs in an isolated sandbox and opens a PR; or point Claude Code at the repo — a web session at claude.ai/code, or an @claude mention on the issue via the GitHub Actions integration — to do the same.
Track progress from the Codex task list if you're running more than one task at once, or from the Claude Code session or PR thread for a single task.
When the PR opens, read the description it generates first — it should restate what it built against your acceptance criteria.
Review the diff and the CI checks exactly as you would a human contributor's PR: no lowered bar because an agent wrote it.
Leave PR review comments for anything wrong or missing — both Codex and Claude Code can read and respond to review comments on their own PR.
Merge only once acceptance criteria are met and checks pass, and let the merge close the issue, not the other way around.
lessons.prompt:
Title: Add rate limiting to the public search endpoint

Problem: /api/search has no rate limiting, so a single client can hammer it and degrade the service for everyone.

Acceptance criteria:
1. Limit each API key to 30 requests/minute on /api/search.
2. Requests over the limit return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
3. The limit is configurable via an environment variable, not hardcoded.
4. Add tests covering: under-limit requests succeed, over-limit requests get 429, and the Retry-After value is correct.

Scope: only touch src/middleware/ and src/routes/search.ts. Do not add a new database table — use the existing Redis client in src/lib/redis.ts for the counter.

Out of scope: rate limiting other endpoints (separate issue).
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable issue template — hand off to a Codex cloud task or Claude Code
lessons.explanation: Numbered acceptance criteria give whichever tool you hand this to a checklist it can satisfy and give you a checklist to verify the PR against — vague issues produce plausible-looking PRs that miss half of what you actually needed. The explicit scope line keeps the agent from reaching for a new dependency or reinventing rate limiting from scratch. The 'out of scope' line matters just as much: it stops either tool from 'helpfully' expanding the task into something bigger and harder to review.
lessons.example:
Input: the issue above, handed to a Codex cloud task (or, run the same issue through Claude Code for comparison).

Typical output: within some minutes, a draft PR touching exactly the two named locations, using the existing Redis client for a sliding-window counter, returning 429 with Retry-After, reading the limit from an env var with a sensible default, and including the three requested test cases — reviewable against the acceptance criteria line by line.
lessons.exercise: In your own repository, write one real, small, well-scoped issue using the template above for a task you'd genuinely delegate. Run it as a Codex cloud task, and if you want the comparison, run a duplicate issue through Claude Code — when each PR arrives, check off every acceptance criterion against the actual diff before approving or requesting changes.
lessons.expectedResult: A draft PR you can evaluate criterion by criterion in a few minutes, with review comments (if any) that the agent can act on directly in the same thread.
commonMistakes: Writing the issue as a one-line request ('add rate limiting') and getting back a PR that solves a different, more generic version of the problem than the one you actually had.
Skipping scope boundaries, then discovering the agent added a new dependency or touched an unrelated file to solve the problem its own way.
Reviewing an agent-authored PR less critically than a human one, on the assumption that 'the AI already checked it' — it did not check business context only you have.
Assigning genuinely ambiguous or under-specified problems (ones a human teammate would need a meeting to scope) and blaming the agent for guessing wrong.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running template of your team's best-performing issue format — problem, acceptance criteria, scope, out-of-scope — and require it for any issue you intend to delegate, whichever of the two tools ends up doing the work.

lessons.title: Catch issues before a human has to: Codex review and Claude Code's /code-review
lessons.summary: Use Codex's automatic PR review or Claude Code's /code-review and /review commands as a first pass on pull requests, read the comments critically, and combine them with human review instead of replacing it.
lessons.goal: Use AI code review — Codex on GitHub PRs, or Claude Code's /code-review and /review slash commands — as a first pass on pull requests, verifying flagged issues instead of trusting them at face value.
lessons.whyItMatters: Codex's GitHub review runs automatically on PRs once enabled for a repo, commenting the way a fast first reviewer would. Claude Code's /code-review can target the current diff, a PR number, a branch, or a path, at a chosen effort level, and can post inline comments or apply fixes directly with --fix. Both draw on real code execution, not just a pattern-matched diff, which catches more real bugs — but using either well means treating it as a fast, imperfect first reviewer, not a substitute for a human sign-off.
steps: Enable Codex as an automatic reviewer on pull requests in your repository settings, or run Claude Code's /code-review locally against the current diff, a specific PR number, or a branch.
Wait for the review to complete — an agentic pass that actually exercises the code takes longer than a simple diff scan, so don't expect it instantly on a large PR.
Read each comment's rationale, not just its headline — a useful review explains why it flagged something, which is what lets you judge whether it's right.
Verify any flagged logic issue by actually checking the code path yourself or running the relevant test, rather than trusting the flag at face value.
Accept valid suggestions directly where a one-click fix is offered; with Claude Code you can also pass --fix to apply the findings to your working tree.
Dismiss false positives with a short reasoning comment explaining why the flagged pattern is intentional — this also improves the quality of the next pass on the same repo.
Always pair either tool's pass with at least one human reviewer for anything touching business logic, security, or public APIs — treat the AI pass as pre-review, not final review.
If Codex review runs on every PR in an active repo, or you're running Claude Code review at a higher effort level than the default, keep an eye on usage — a deeper pass costs more than a quick one.
lessons.prompt: Review this PR with particular attention to: 1) whether the new /cancel endpoint checks authorization before checking order status, 2) whether the Redis counter has a race condition under concurrent requests, 3) whether any of the new error paths leak internal details in the response body.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable review focus — post as a PR comment for Codex, or pass as the focus to Claude Code's /code-review
lessons.explanation: A general 'review this PR' request gets a general pass; naming the three specific risk areas — authorization ordering, a concurrency race, and information leakage — directs either tool to actually exercise those code paths instead of skimming past them. This mirrors how you'd brief a human reviewer on what worries you most about a change, and it tends to surface the review comments that matter instead of a long list of low-value style notes.
lessons.example:
Input: the focus above, posted on a PR implementing the cancel endpoint from a previous lesson, run through Codex's automatic review (or Claude Code's /code-review with the same focus).

Typical output: a comment confirming the authorization check runs before the status check (or flagging that it doesn't), a note on whether the Redis increment-and-check is atomic or has a check-then-act race, and a check of the 409 response body for any leaked internal error messages — each with a one-line rationale you can verify by opening the diff.
lessons.exercise: On a real pull request in your own repository, request a review from Codex or run Claude Code's /code-review, pointing it at one specific risk you're genuinely unsure about. Read its comment's rationale, verify it yourself against the code, and either accept the suggestion or leave a reasoned dismissal.
lessons.expectedResult: At least one review comment you can independently verify as correct or incorrect within a few minutes, rather than a list of comments you accept or ignore on faith.
commonMistakes: Treating an approving AI review as equivalent to human sign-off and merging without any human reviewer on a change that touches business logic or security.
Dismissing every AI comment as noise without reading the rationale, missing the real catches mixed in with lower-value ones.
Requesting review with no specific focus on a large, high-risk PR, then being surprised the pass reads more like a style check than a deep analysis.
Not tracking how much a deeper review pass costs on either tool, then getting surprised by usage on an active team repository.
lessons.proTip: On your highest-risk repositories (payments, auth, data access), keep a short list of the 3-4 categories of bug that have actually bitten your team before, and reference that list explicitly in every review request — it turns either tool's review into institutional memory instead of a generic pass.

lessons.title: Write CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and .cursor/rules so every tool follows your team's standards
lessons.summary: Create repo-level instruction files — a canonical AGENTS.md plus CLAUDE.md and .cursor/rules — that shape Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor to your team's actual conventions instead of generic defaults.
lessons.goal: Write project instruction files that encode your repository's stack, conventions, and hard constraints so every tool's suggestions follow them automatically, without three teams maintaining three contradictory documents.
lessons.whyItMatters: Without instructions, each tool suggests generically reasonable code that may not match your team's actual stack version, error-handling convention, or banned dependencies. Three tools read three different file formats — but they don't have to be three separate documents: AGENTS.md is read natively by Codex and by Cursor as ambient project context, and Claude Code can import it into CLAUDE.md with a single line, so you maintain one source of truth instead of three copies that quietly drift apart.
steps: Write AGENTS.md at the repository root as your canonical instructions file — Codex reads it automatically, and Cursor reads it as ambient project context.
In CLAUDE.md, pull the same content in with a single line — `@AGENTS.md` — instead of duplicating it; Claude Code resolves the import at the start of every session.

For Cursor-specific behavior (scoping a rule to certain file types, or making it always-on instead of contextual), add a short file at .cursor/rules/*.mdc with YAML frontmatter (description, alwaysApply, globs) that points back to the same conventions rather than restating them.
State the stack precisely: language and framework versions, not just names (e.g. 'React 19 with Server Components,' not just 'React').
List positive conventions: naming patterns, error-handling approach, how tests are structured, where shared utilities live — point at real files, not abstractions.
List hard 'do not' rules: banned libraries, patterns the team has deliberately moved away from, anything that must never be introduced without a human decision.
Keep it short and specific — a long file of generic best practices gets skimmed by a model the same way it would by a human; specific, repo-true statements carry more weight.
Verify it's working by asking an ordinary question in each tool you use and checking whether the answer follows a convention stated in the file.
Revisit and update the file when conventions change — a stale instructions file actively misleads every tool that reads it.
lessons.prompt:
# AGENTS.md for this repository

Stack: TypeScript 5.x, Next.js 15 (App Router), PostgreSQL via Prisma. No pages router code — this is Server Components only.

Conventions:
- All API responses use the shared `ApiResult<T>` type from src/lib/types.ts — never return raw objects.
- Errors are thrown as subclasses of AppError (src/lib/errors.ts), never plain Error.
- Every new database query goes through the repository layer in src/repositories/, never Prisma calls inline in route handlers.

Do not:
- Add new npm dependencies without flagging it explicitly for human approval.
- Use moment.js or date-fns — this repo uses the native Temporal API only.
- Modify prisma/schema.prisma as part of an unrelated feature change.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable AGENTS.md starting point — import into CLAUDE.md with `@AGENTS.md`
lessons.explanation: Naming exact versions and the App Router constraint stops any of the three tools from suggesting Pages Router patterns that technically work in older Next.js but are wrong for this repo. The three positive conventions point at concrete files instead of describing them abstractly, which is what lets a model actually apply them rather than approximate them. The 'do not' section closes off specific wrong choices this team has already made and rejected once — and because AGENTS.md is the single file all three tools resolve back to, closing it off once closes it off everywhere.
lessons.example:
Input: the AGENTS.md above, present in a repo where a developer asks any of the three tools to add a new endpoint returning order data.

Typical output: a route handler that wraps its response in ApiResult<Order>, throws an OrderNotFoundError subclassing AppError instead of a plain Error, and calls into a new or existing method on an orders repository file instead of writing a raw Prisma query directly in the route — the same answer whichever of the three tools produced it, because each one resolved back to the same source.
lessons.exercise: In one of your own repositories, write an AGENTS.md with your actual stack versions, 2-3 real conventions (pointing at real files), and at least one genuine 'do not' rule your team already enforces in code review. If you use Claude Code, add `@AGENTS.md` to CLAUDE.md. Ask an ordinary question in whichever of the three tools you use and check whether the answer reflects the file.
lessons.expectedResult: A suggestion or chat answer that follows at least one stated convention correctly without you having to mention it in the prompt itself — and the same answer regardless of which of the three tools you asked.
commonMistakes: Writing generic best-practice advice ('write clean code,' 'use meaningful names') instead of repo-specific facts — generic advice doesn't change behavior because it doesn't disambiguate anything.
Writing three separate instructions files by hand instead of one canonical AGENTS.md, and letting them drift out of sync so each tool quietly gives a different answer to the same question.
Letting the file go stale after a framework upgrade or a convention change, so it now actively contradicts the current codebase.
Making the file too long, burying the two or three rules that actually matter under a wall of aspirational guidelines nobody enforces.
lessons.proTip: Add one line to the 'do not' section every time an AI-generated suggestion violates a convention your team cares about — treat AGENTS.md as a living record of mistakes you've already paid for once and don't want to pay for again, in any of the three tools.

lessons.title: Roll out a consistent AI coding workflow across claude-code, codex, and cursor
lessons.summary: Decide which tool handles which kind of work, keep concurrent agent tasks visible across three separate systems, and manage three subscriptions deliberately so a team adopts AI coding tools on purpose instead of by accident.
lessons.goal: Stand up team-level infrastructure across Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor — a shared tool-selection policy, a habit of tracking concurrent agent work across all three, and a usage-budgeting habit — so adoption is consistent across the team rather than left to each individual.
lessons.whyItMatters: Individual developers get value from any one of these tools with zero coordination. A team gets compounding value only when there's an actual policy for which tool handles which kind of work, when concurrent agent work is visible somewhere instead of scattered across three separate task lists, and when someone is watching three separate billing surfaces instead of getting surprised by whichever one spiked that month.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Admin or billing visibility on at least a Claude Team, ChatGPT Business, and Cursor Business/Teams plan for the parts of the workflow you intend to standardize.
steps: Write down, in one page, which tool is the default for which kind of work: Cursor for hands-on daily coding and Tab-driven completions, Claude Code for deep investigation and CI-integrated review, Codex cloud tasks for well-scoped issue-to-PR delegation you can walk away from — and let people deviate with a reason, not enforce it rigidly.
Point every repo at the shared AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursor/rules setup from the previous lesson so the policy is encoded, not just written down somewhere people forget to read.

When multiple people are running concurrent agent work, agree on where it's visible: Codex's cloud task list, Cursor's background/cloud agent queue, and Claude Code's session list are three separate places — pick a lightweight habit (a shared doc, a channel, or checking all three each morning) rather than assuming everyone already knows what's in flight.
Use git worktrees (Claude Code's `-w` flag, or a plain worktree checkout) when more than one agent needs to work in the same repository at once, so parallel sessions don't collide on the same branch.
Set repo- or org-level access policy on each tool matching your risk tolerance — which repos a Codex cloud task or Claude Code background session is allowed to touch, and which stay hands-on-only.

Review usage across all three subscriptions monthly, not just one: Claude's 5-hour/weekly caps, Codex's rolling 5-hour window and token credits, and Cursor's usage-credit pool all meter differently, and a spike in one doesn't show up in the others.
Set a team norm explicitly, in your contribution guidelines and not just as an assumption: agent-authored PRs from any of the three tools get the same review bar as human-authored ones.
lessons.prompt:
Team AI coding policy — one page

Default tool by task:
- Day-to-day coding, completions, small edits: Cursor (Tab + Agent)
- Deep investigation, planning, CI-integrated review: Claude Code
- Well-scoped issue -> PR, run unattended: Codex cloud tasks

Shared instructions: AGENTS.md at repo root, imported into CLAUDE.md via `@AGENTS.md`, referenced from .cursor/rules/team.mdc.

Access policy: Codex cloud tasks and Claude Code background sessions may only run against [repo allowlist]. New repos start hands-on-only until a lead adds them.

Review bar: every agent-authored PR gets at least one human reviewer before merge. No exceptions for passing CI alone.

Usage check-in: first Monday of the month, each lead reviews their team's usage across Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, and Cursor billing pages and reports anything trending toward a plan upgrade.
lessons.promptLabel: Copyable one-page team AI coding policy
lessons.explanation: Naming defaults up front prevents a per-task argument about which tool to use every single time. The access-policy line matters because it's the difference between an unattended agent reaching only the repos it's supposed to and one that technically could reach further. The review-bar line matters because it's the thing everyone assumes is already agreed until the day it isn't. And the usage check-in catches a spike on whichever of the three separate billing systems is actually trending upward, instead of everyone assuming someone else is watching it.
lessons.example:
Input: the policy above, shared in a team's onboarding channel.

Typical outcome: a new hire reads it in two minutes, starts hands-on work in Cursor by default, knows to escalate a large refactor to a dedicated Claude Code session, and delegates a well-scoped backlog cleanup ticket to a Codex cloud task — without asking a senior engineer which tool to reach for.
lessons.exercise: Write a one-page version of this policy for a real team you're part of, or a side project you treat like one. Name the actual repos in the access-policy line, and set a real date for the monthly usage check-in. Share it somewhere your team will actually see it.
lessons.expectedResult: A policy a new teammate could read in under five minutes and immediately know which tool to reach for, with the review bar and usage habits stated instead of assumed.
commonMistakes: Never writing the default-tool policy down, so every developer picks based on habit and the team ends up with three inconsistent sets of conventions.
Skipping the access-policy line, so an unattended Codex cloud task or Claude Code background session has the same reach into a sensitive repo as into a low-risk one.
Only discovering a usage spike after the bill arrives, on whichever of the three billing pages nobody was checking that month.
Treating agent-authored PRs as lower-scrutiny than human ones once the novelty wears off, quietly lowering the review bar the policy was supposed to hold.
lessons.proTip: Name one person per team as the owner of that team's shared AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/.cursor/rules setup and the monthly usage check-in — not a full-time role, just an accountable owner, so the policy stays current instead of becoming everyone's job and no one's.
